problem: Prior multi-LLM QA work (voting, debate, mixture of experts) assumes zero-shot questions or provided information sources, and does not handle QA about an unknown environment that must first be explored, where each agent has only partial observations.
motivation: Household embodied assistants must answer questions about their environment, and a single agent with a limited field of view explores poorly. Multiple explorers cover more ground, but their answers conflict. Voting and debate are also vulnerable to wrong or malicious agents.
key_idea: Have several LLM agents explore a Matterport3D house independently, then aggregate their binary answers with a supervised central answer model (CAM) trained on [object, room, agent answers] instead of majority vote or debate.
insight: A learned aggregator can correct systematic agent errors that voting and debate cannot. Debate is often slightly worse than MV because correct agents get swayed by wrong ones. XGBoost agrees with the agents far less (about 38%) than MV does (about 95%), which means it learns to override unreliable answers. The permutation feature importance analysis shows CAM ignores an agent whose answers are 91.5% 'No'. Caveat: the CAM is trained per environment, and much of its gain may come from the object/room query features and dataset label structure rather than from agent reasoning.
method: Exploration: 3 GPT-4-turbo agents each run 10 steps of a modified LGX (Language-Guided Exploration) on the Matterport3D topological graph with an 'aggressively explore' prompt; GLIP-detected items per node are stored as observations.
Query generation: 'Is there an o in room r?' binary questions. Yes-labels come from GLIP detections per room; No-labels come from the same item paired with a random room that does not contain it.
QA phase: each agent is prompted with its observation dictionary {room: [items]} and told to combine common sense with its observations, answering YES or NO.
Non-learning aggregation: majority vote, or a 2-round turn-based debate followed by a majority vote of the final answers.
CAM: a classifier over the (2+K)-dim input [object, room, K agent answers], trained per environment. Variants: NN (16-8-1), RF (1000 trees), DT, XGBoost, RBF SVM, linear SVM, LR.
Analysis: permutation feature importance, agent-to-final-answer agreement, and a malicious-agent test in which one agent's answers are inverted.

setting.backbone: GPT-4-turbo (frozen) agents for exploration and QA; sklearn/XGBoost/small NN classifiers as CAM (trained from scratch)
setting.training_data: Per-environment synthetic Yes/No query set built from GLIP detections on Matterport3D scans; 90%/10% random train/test split, 5 seeds
setting.observation: Topological graph nodes of Matterport3D, represented as GLIP-detected object lists per room (text)
setting.action_space: discrete nav-graph node hops (10 steps of LGX)
setting.privileged: Ground-truth labels for CAM training. GLIP detections define the labels. The feature-importance and appendix experiments use oracle exploration.

numbers.eval_set_note: 10% random held-out queries, mean over 5 seeds; 215-node environment
numbers.extra: 3 LGX agents, 10 steps; per-environment trained aggregator
numbers.evidence: Table 1, 215 nodes row, XG column: 88.33 (MV 42.00, Debate 43.00)

numbers_note: Table 1 gives accuracy for 8 environments (20 to 215 nodes) and all CAM variants. Only the best variant per key environment is listed here. This is a custom benchmark, not a standard navigation benchmark.
results: CAM aggregators beat MV and debate in all 8 environments. XGBoost is best in all but one, reaching 73.33-88.33% against MV/debate at roughly 40-59%, which is up to about 46 points higher. With a malicious agent, CAM still outperforms MV and debate.
limitations: Requires ground-truth labels to train a per-environment CAM, which is hard in changing households.
Only objective binary Yes/No object-in-room questions; the labels depend on GLIP detection quality and the negatives are random.
Small setting: 3 agents, 10 exploration steps, topological graph, no real robot; the near-chance MV baseline (about 40-45%) suggests the task or labels are unusual.
